04

Warning · paid-chat social apps

The first three sections are "worth a look"; this one is "been there". It has one entry so far, an account of the owner's own experience, with no external links, plus two original screenshots of the comment section from back then.

Platform warning · the owner's experience

Soul: the ban was a separate, earlier matter; chatting up or messaging women now costs money

Ban around 2017 or 2018 · this "Moment" post 2019 or 2020 (the owner cannot remember either)Source: the owner's own accountScope: personal experience and observation, not a data check

First, keep two matters apart. The owner's "Moment" post was in 2019 or 2020 (he cannot recall); there was indeed a heated argument under it, but it was between people in the comment section,the owner did not argue with anyone under that post. The dispute the owner had around that time was with someone in private messages, and is a different matter from this post.

The ban was an even earlier matter, around 2017 or 2018 — also unclear. The ban is one thing and this post is another; they are not the same and must not be strung together into "he argued under a Moment post, so he was banned". He did not simply let it go: he filed feedback and contacted the administrators. An administrator replied in the back office with one line, verbatim:

"So because you were afraid of being criticised, you acted aggressively towards others first — do you think that is correct behaviour?"

This site does not reword that line. It is exactly the reply the owner received after filing feedback; there was no further explanation of how the report was upheld or under which rule it was handled.What is described here is that earlier ban, unrelated to the "Moment" post above or the comment-section argument.The ban was carried out unilaterally by the platform from start to finish: who reported, how it was judged, how the appeal was answered — the user received only an outcome and a rhetorical question.

And now, for men to strike up a conversation or message a woman, it is paid. The owner's own words:

Does that not amount to the platform assuming men ought to spend money on women, play the simp, and indulging the simp economy?

This site lists it under "warnings" not to pass judgement on a platform, but because two things happen to line up:On one side, a product design where men must pay before they can speak; on the other, unequal handling and appeals once something goes wrong.The pricing gives the platform an interest in "whoever wants to talk pays", so it has no incentive to make the terms of communication more equal; and when conflict does arise, the judgement is not in the user's hands.

The owner also offers a comparison across time: back in 2017 and 2018, Soul, Tantan and Momo were still fairly normal — at least the women were. The social apps that came later are hard to describe in a sentence; meeting one decent person already counts as the best possible ending.

So what exactly is being avoided here?
  1. Do not pay for "the right to speak". Once chatting, private messages or approaches are charged per use or per permission tier, ask first whether you are buying a service or an expectation that was designed into you.
  2. Do not automatically read a ban as proof you were in the wrong, and do not keep escalating while emotions run high. Keep your own record of what you said; in an appeal, state only facts. A platform's reply is not a finding of fact.
  3. Treat "meeting someone you can talk to normally" as a good outcome, not a default setting. If it is not there, leave — there is no need to persuade anyone.

Two screenshots of the comment section from back then (originals kept)

Page screenshots saved by the owner in 2019 or 2020 (he cannot recall), shown as-is: no cropping, no altered text. Click an image to enlarge it. Only encrypted files are stored in the repository; the browser decrypts them locally, and the page exposes no static image URLs.

About the people in the images:The poster, the commenters and every avatar and nickname in the screenshots belong to other users of the platform at the time;not one of them is the owner; the women's accounts and avatars shown are not the owner either. The entry whose nickname reads "Me" is the logged-in account marker of the device that took the screenshot; this site does not use it to identify anyone.The owner took no part in the argument under this post — the people arguing there were others; the ban was an earlier, separate matter and has nothing to do with these two images.No account is named or identified here, and the aggressive wording in the comments is not repeated. The two images only show that this argument did take place under that post, and what the tone of the comment section was like; they are not an assessment of anyone.

Scope and limits:This section is based on the owner's spoken first-hand experience and observation. This site has not independently verified Soul's current pricing, reporting or ban rules; whatever the app shows in real time is authoritative. Per the owner's correction of 2026-11-07, the ban (around 2017/2018) and this "Moment" post with its comment argument (2019/2020) are two independent events; this page draws no causal link and does not place the owner among the comment-section disputants. The two screenshots above are kept as-is at the owner's request of 2026-11-06; this site names or identifies no account in them and does not repeat the aggressive wording in the comments. The images are retained only as a record of that argument at the time, not as a finding of fact. The first three sections are recommendations; this one is a warning, and the two are not mixed — this section carries no purchase, sign-up or download links. As stated site-wide, this is personal experience and judgement, not an overall assessment of the platform, any institution or any group.
